text: Motors use half the world's electricity, and most of them run at speeds nobody ever checked against their own resonances. Argonaut turns any camera into a vibration analyst. Pick a machine, upload your footage, or connect a live feed.

A hand-held walk around a real motor and pump. Muse Spark names each part and what it does. SAM 3.1 tracks it, so the outline stays on the motor housing, then the baseplate, as the camera moves. Every reading is measured inside that moving mask, with the camera's own motion subtracted.

Now a factory fan, starting up. Muse Spark counts six blades. A Bayesian model then weighs every line in this sound against what a six-blade fan can produce, and answers 413 rpm, with 97 percent probability. Without the blade count, the same sound reads 2477.
The same engine runs on belts, mine conveyors, pumps and a motor test bench. Where the evidence is ambiguous, it says so instead of guessing. And anyone can upload their own video.

Then the agents act. Muse Wonder calls tools and decides the fix. Here it field-balances a pump: it measures the vibration vector, fits a trial weight, and computes the correction, 18.9 grams at 211 degrees. One-times vibration falls 84 percent, inside the ISO limit. It writes the work order and books the re-check. A person approves every step. This one ran on our simulated drive.
It also runs the machine better: out of resonance, then re-measured. Vibration fell 89 percent on the simulated plant, and every number the agent writes is checked against the measurements.

That spoken command, in Hindi and English together, went through Muse Voice Transcribe and started this analysis. The agent then reasoned on the open-weight Muse Spark Open, which a plant can host itself.

Five Meta models, each with one job. SAM 3.1 is the sensors. Muse Spark is the eyes: it names parts, counts blades and reads nameplates. Muse Wonder is the engineer. Voice Transcribe is the ears. Muse Spark Open keeps data private. Then five agent actions: field balance, drive skip bands, the work order, the cost impact, and the follow-up that proves it worked.
